Pokémon. A multimedia franchise launched by Nintendo and Game Freak in 1996, centered on capturing, training, and battling creatures called Pokémon. Beginning as a pair of Game Boy titles, it exploded into a global phenomenon spanning games, trading cards, films, and merchandise, becoming one of the highest-grossing media franchises of all time. The series debuted with Pokémon Red and Pokémon Blue in 1996 on Game Boy, where players travel as trainers catching and training Pokémon to battle each other, gym leaders, and ultimately the Elite Four and Champion.

The core mechanic involves Pokémon with different types like Fire, Water, Grass, and Electric. Each has moves with different power and accuracy, and evolution lines—a Charmander evolves into Charmeleon, then Charizard, gaining stats and new moves. The original games featured one hundred fifty-one Pokémon counting Mew as a secret, and each generation adds new species. Over one thousand Pokémon exist across ten generations of main-series games. Trading is central to the experience. Red and Blue could only catch different Pokémon subsets, forcing players to trade to complete their Pokédex, a codex of all encountered species.

Pikachu, the franchise mascot, is Ash Ketchum's companion in the long-running anime that started in 1997 and continues to the present. The trading card game, which also began in 1996 and continues today, creates a parallel collecting economy. Main-series games span Nintendo handhelds from Game Boy through Switch and consoles. Spin-offs include Pokémon GO, a mobile augmented-reality game from 2016, mystery dungeon games, and Pokémon Legends: Arceus. Recent entries like Sword and Shield and Scarlet and Violet offer open-world exploration and dynamic difficulty, moving away from strictly linear gym progression. Game Freak developed the games alongside Nintendo as publisher and rights holder, while trading card games form a parallel billion-dollar collectible card economy.
